Petrelintide (ZP8396): Amylin Receptor Agonist with Best-in-Class Tolerability — Research Dossier

Research compounds discussed for educational purposes. Not FDA-approved for human use where applicable. Consult a healthcare provider before use.

What Is Petrelintide?

Petrelintide (ZP8396) is an investigational once-weekly injectable amylin receptor agonist developed by Zealand Pharma under a major Phase 3 partnership with Roche. It is a synthetic analog of amylin — a small peptide hormone co-secreted with insulin from pancreatic beta cells — engineered for a once-weekly pharmacokinetic profile. Unlike the GLP-1 receptor agonist class (semaglutide, tirzepatide, retatrutide), petrelintide does not activate GLP-1 or glucagon receptors at all. It acts exclusively on amylin receptors, primarily in the brainstem's area postrema, to suppress appetite and slow gastric emptying through a completely independent neural pathway.

This mechanistic independence from the GLP-1 pathway is the defining feature of petrelintide: the persistent nausea and vomiting associated with GLP-1 agonists is largely mediated by GLP-1 receptor activation in the gut and brainstem. By bypassing the GLP-1 receptor entirely, petrelintide achieves meaningful weight loss with a GI adverse event profile that, in Phase 2, was statistically indistinguishable from placebo.

Mechanism of Action

  • Amylin receptor agonism: Activates calcitonin receptor / receptor activity-modifying protein (RAMP) complexes in the brainstem's area postrema, a region known as the chemosensory trigger zone. This reduces food intake and slows gastric emptying.
  • No GLP-1R or GCGR activity: Does not engage hypothalamic GLP-1 pathways or hepatic glucagon receptor pathways, which distinguishes it from all major marketed obesity drugs and pipeline candidates except pramlintide.
  • Pancreatic effects: Suppresses post-meal glucagon secretion (contributing to glucose control in T2D), complements insulin action, and reduces post-meal glucose excursions.
  • Tolerability mechanism: Because GI effects of amylin agonism primarily operate through central brainstem circuits (not peripheral GI GLP-1 receptors), the typical GLP-1-class nausea profile is absent or markedly attenuated.

Key Research Findings

ZUPREME-1 — Obesity Without Type 2 Diabetes

  • Population: Adults with overweight or obesity without T2D
  • Duration: 42 weeks
  • Weight loss: Up to 10.7% vs 1.7% placebo (efficacy estimand)
  • GI tolerability: Adverse events at rates comparable to placebo — the key differentiator from GLP-1 class drugs
  • Publication: The Lancet Diabetes & Endocrinology, September 29, 2026; presented at EASD 2026

ZUPREME-2 — Obesity With Type 2 Diabetes

  • Population: 220 adults with overweight/obesity and type 2 diabetes
  • Duration: 28 weeks
  • Weight loss: Up to 9.2% vs 2.0% placebo at Week 28
  • HbA1c: Reduced by up to 0.65% vs a placebo increase
  • Discontinuations due to AEs: 1.9% (petrelintide) vs 1.7% (placebo) — virtually identical
  • Topline announced: October 7, 2026; Zealand Pharma press release
  • Analyst note: Blood sugar improvement described as less impressive than glucose-lowering drugs, though the mechanism is not designed primarily as a diabetes therapy

Phase 3 with Roche

Zealand Pharma announced a major Phase 3 partnership with Roche based on the Phase 2 data. Phase 3 is now underway, with Roche providing development infrastructure and global regulatory expertise. This partnership significantly de-risks the program and accelerates the timeline to potential approval.

How Does Petrelintide Compare to Cagrilintide?

Both are once-weekly amylin analogs, but they are distinct molecules with different pharmacokinetic profiles. Cagrilintide (Novo Nordisk) is most advanced in the CagriSema combination (cagrilintide + semaglutide), which targets both amylin and GLP-1 receptors simultaneously. Petrelintide is being developed as a standalone amylin agonist and — importantly — may also become a combination partner with GLP-1 drugs in the future, where its tolerability profile could counterbalance the GI burden of higher GLP-1 doses.

Frequently Asked Questions

What makes petrelintide different from GLP-1 drugs like semaglutide?

Petrelintide is a pure amylin receptor agonist — completely distinct from the GLP-1 receptor pathway. Phase 2 (ZUPREME-1 and ZUPREME-2) showed GI adverse events at placebo rates, unlike GLP-1 drugs where 30-40% of patients experience nausea during dose escalation. Weight loss in Phase 2 (10.7%; 9.2% in T2D) is somewhat lower than GLP-1 agonists at comparable timepoints, but the tolerability profile makes petrelintide an option for patients intolerant to GLP-1 drugs, and a potential combination partner.

Has petrelintide been approved anywhere?

No. As of October 2026, petrelintide is fully investigational. Phase 2 ZUPREME-1 results were published in The Lancet Diabetes & Endocrinology (September 2026) and ZUPREME-2 positive topline results were announced October 7, 2026. Phase 3 is underway with Roche. It should only be used in authorized clinical trial protocols.

Is petrelintide related to pramlintide or cagrilintide?

All three are amylin analogs. Pramlintide (FDA-approved, short-acting, multiple daily injections). Cagrilintide (Novo Nordisk, once-weekly, primarily studied as CagriSema combination). Petrelintide (Zealand/Roche, once-weekly, standalone, best GI tolerability in Phase 2). They share the amylin receptor target but differ in structure, half-life, and clinical profile.

Research Limitations

  • No regulatory approval — Phase 3 program just underway as of October 2026
  • Weight loss (~9-11% in Phase 2) is lower than top-performing GLP-1 agents (20-22%) at comparable timepoints
  • ZUPREME-2 HbA1c reduction was modest compared to diabetes-specific drugs (0.65%)
  • Long-term cardiovascular safety and outcomes data not yet available
  • Phase 3 duration will likely require 2+ years before readout and regulatory filing
